text.p: Further to our reports on the move of the Labor opposition away from the economic rationalist policies pursued by Paul Keating, opposition industry spokesman Simon Crean recently gave an interesting address to a conference in Coolum, Queensland.
In it, he set out a position which was implicitly critical of the Keating government's policies, but as we have remarked before, this cannot be avoided if a big policy change is underway.

Crean said, in part: "The reality is we need a more active industry policy, one which recognises the limits of the free market philosophy, one which actively encourages and supports the manufacturing sector.
"It is not good enough to simply urge industry to become more competitive and productive -- we have to assist them to become so.
"Whilst we worked so well to remove the old protective policy regime and open up the economy with impressive results to date, we must do more now to develop the new policy regime."
Crean added that the debate on industry policy had been debased to a simplified choice between the free market and intervention.
"My argument is that we need to look at these issues strategically, not polemically."
It is stating the obvious to say that executives in industry would wish that Labor had come to this realisation whilst in government, not in opposition.
But at least Crean and his colleagues are widening the policy gap between the opposition and the Howard government.
With Treasury running unchallenged as the government's policy adviser, virtually all of the industry-specific programmes for industry have been abolished.
John Howard passionately believes that all he needs to do for industry is get the industrial relations package through the Senate.
Once this is done, everything else will fall into place.
Our own contacts with industry representatives suggest that most believe and strongly support the industrial relations package.
But they do not believe that, of itself, it will solve Australia's unemployment problems and lead to a burgeoning of exports. (They are not, incidentally, saying this publicly.)
(Views are those of Inside Canberra, not Reuters)
